The BVPV Styrenics Painesville site occupies 55 acres in Painesville, Ohio (approximately 30 miles east of Cleveland). The site is bordered on the north by a residential area, with Lake Erie approximately one-half mile to the north. The area south of the site is industrial. The nearest residence abuts the north property line. There are no schools or hospitals within three miles of the site.

Currently, there are 44 full-time BVPV Styrenics employees working in manufacturing, technology and administrative jobs at the site.

The Painesville site is a global leader in the production of plastic resin for polystyrene foams. The major product is expandable polystyrene.

The BVPV Styrenics Painesville site's approach to chemical safety is best described by the BVPV Styrenics EHS&S  (Safety, Health, Environment Protection, Quality, and Sustainability) Policy Statement, that begins with the following statement and goes on to list guiding principles of conduct:

Styropek  is a chemical company, where all collaborators are committed to the highest standards of safety, health, environmental protection, quality and sustainability according to:
	The Values and Code of Conduct.
	The required quality by our clients in products, services and solutions.
	Achieving business excellence through:
o	Continuous improvement.
o	Risk analysis.
o	Environmental protection.
o	The management of our operations and processes in a sustainable manner under the ESG (Environment, Social and Governance) criteria.

With the active participation and interaction of all interested parties in order to achieve:
	Preserved health and integrity of collaborators.
	Increased customer satisfaction.
	Promoting Sustainable Development.
	Compliance with national, international and voluntary government regulations.
	Standardize our ESG strategy, thus, contribute to sustainable development where we live and operate.

We fulfill this policy commitment through the application of a comprehensive EHS&S management

system that ensures:
	Identifiable EHS&S risks associated with BVPV Styrenics businesses, operations and products are assessed and successfully managed.
	Safety, health and environmental laws, regulations, and permit requirements are followed or exceeded.
	Appropriate policies, programs and procedures are in place and continuous employee learning opportunities are available.
	Best available science, technology and industry practices are being applied with due consideration given to economics and technical practicality.
	Organizational responsibilities are clearly defined, understood and carried out and every employee is responsible and accountable for BVPV Styrenics performance.
	Systems are in place to ensure that EHS&S policies, standards and procedures are being followed and that performance is measured against the best in the industry.
	Change, whether it be in leadership, organization, chemical or business processes, is managed in a way that maintains, or if possible, enhances EHS&S performance.

We only engage in business with companies that demonstrate a commitment to EHS&S practices. 

BVPV Styrenics EHS&S performance is communicated to all stakeholders.
Excellence in EHS&S performance is everyone's responsibility. All employees must adopt and encourage safe work practices and conduct all work-related activities in an environmentally responsible manner. Leaders in all facilities and business units are accountable for their organization's EHS&S performance and for achieving satisfactory performance from their customers, suppliers, carriers and contractors.

BVPV Styrenics the Painesville Site is required to comply with the 40 CR 68, Risk Management Program (RMP) because pentane is a listed chemical in RMP and is used in our manufacturing processes in amounts above the threshold quantity (TQ). Pentane is used to produce expandable polystyrene resin (EPS) that is manufactured at the site. Our resin is in bead form and is sent to customers that mold the

beads into end products (i.e., packaging or insulating materials).
Pentane is piped through a closed system from a 47,000-gallon storage tank into vessels in the process area. Pentane is potentially used during two parts of the process, initially during bead formation then occasionally later during the drying stage as a paste applied to the beads to provide lubrication for customer processing. Pentane is delivered to the site in rail cars.
Pentane vapors are collected during the process in a spherical gas ball and sent to one of two boilers for destruction.

Worst-case release scenario
EPA has defined a worst-case release as the release of the largest quantity of a regulated substance that results in the greatest distance from the point of release to a specified end point. At the Painesville site, the only regulated substance used on-site is pentane, which possesses the characteristic of flammability. The Worst-Case release scenario requirement for flammables considers liquids at the highest ambient temperature in the last three years, which was 91.4 deg F, and the amount of those liquids that becomes vapor in the first 10 minutes of the release. This is used to determine the endpoint during a vapor cloud explosion.
Applying the worst-case scenario definitions at Painesville, the following information was derived: 
Worst-case scenario involves a release of the maximum quantity of pentane contained in an unmitigated railcar on-site (170,500 lb). The release of this amount of pentane, coupled with a vapor cloud explosion, would result in an estimated distance to 1 pound per square inch (psi) overpressure of 0.4 miles. RMP*Comp, supplied by the EPA, was the technique/software used to determine the overpressure end point. On the basis of this distance and considering the population density of Painesville Township, Ohio, it is estimated that there would be 877 residential receptors in this area (mostly north of the facility). There are no environmental receptors in this

area.

Alternative Release Case Scenario
The processes involving pentane at the site were studied to develop the alternate case scenario. The facility utilized the knowledge of the process operators and engineers to develop an alternate case scenario that would be more likely than the worst case scenario. This scenario involves the failure of a 4-inch railcar unloading hose. The area where this would occur has a passive mitigation system consisting of drainage to a gravel dike area, measured to be approximately 7,225 square feet, where released pentane may pool and generate a flammable cloud, which upon ignition, would result in a vapor cloud fire. The scenario involved a release of approximately 44,117 pounds of pentane from a hose rupture for 10 minutes. Passive and active mitigation, including availability of equipment to stop the release and foam suppression, was also considered in the modeling. RMP*Comp was used  and estimated <0.1 miles to the vapor cloud fire end point. This scenario did not produce off site consequences or impacts. A more likely scenario that may cause off site impact could not be found.

Accidental Release Prevention Programs
To prevent the situations described above from occurring, these processes are covered under the OSHA Process Safety Management (PSM) regulations (29 CFR 1910.119). All 14 elements required under the PSM rule are in place at the site and have been integrated into the prevention plan requirements under the Risk Management Program. Compliance with the PSM rule provides the foundation for compliance with the Risk Management Program.
Some of the specific prevention measures in place include the following:
	Presence of pressure relief systems on storage tanks. Dikes surrounding storage tanks.
	On-going equipment inspection programs to monitor mechanical integrity.
	Tanks protected by firewater deluge systems with foam available for vapor suppression in the pentane tank dike. Area classifications that guard against the int

roduction of ignition sources into the process areas.
	Presence of hydrocarbon sensors and alarms to detect pentane releases.
	Continuous monitoring of pentane-unloading operations by operations technicians and frequent facility inspections as part of facility security requirements.

There have been no reportable accidents at the Painesville site involving pentane in the last 5 years  . In fact, pentane has been used at the site for more than 30 years without any major off-site incidents.

To further improve site safety and emergency preparedness, the Painesville Site coordinates its emergency response plan with the Painesville Township Fire Department (PTFD) and the Lake County Emergency Management Agency (EMA). The site conducts periodic pre-plan tours and response drills in conjunction with the PTFD and EMA. Additionally, the site conducts process hazard reviews every 5 years with the last review started and completed in 2023.

The only changes made to this submission over the previous submission pertain to number of employees at the site (44 versus 42), the date of our last process hazard review (2023 versus 2016), consolidation of the rail car unit, and minor updates to wording and storage capacities.
